title: What is the difference between authentication and authorization in IAM, and how does policy evaluation work (explicit deny > explicit allow > implicit deny)?
shortTitle: Authentication versus Authorization and IAM Policy Evaluation
topicTitle: What is the difference between authentication and authorization in IAM, and how

s1_definition.profdef: Authentication is proving who you are — verifying an identity through credentials such as a password, access key signature, or an STS session token. Authorization is deciding what that proven identity is allowed to do — evaluating the applicable IAM policies against the requested action and resource. IAM evaluates authorization by collecting all applicable policies and applying a fixed precedence: an explicit deny always wins, otherwise an explicit allow grants access, and if nothing matches the result is an implicit deny.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, authentication is the guard checking Rajesh's ID card at the entrance to confirm he really is Rajesh. Authorization is the rulebook that then decides which rooms his badge may open. Even if his ID is genuine, a note in the rulebook saying "this person must never enter the vault" overrides every permission — that is the explicit deny winning. If no rule mentions a room at all, the default is that the door stays locked — that is the implicit deny.
s1_definition.oneliner: Authentication proves who you are, authorization decides what you may do, and in IAM an explicit deny beats an explicit allow, which beats the default implicit deny.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Authentication is proving who you are — verifying an identity through credentials such as a password, access key signature, or an STS session token. Authorization is deciding what that proven identity is allowed to do — evaluating the applicable IAM policies against the requested action and resource. IAM evaluates authorization by collecting all applicable policies and applying a fixed precedence: an explicit deny always wins, otherwise an explicit allow grants access, and if nothing matches the result is an implicit deny.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, authentication is the guard checking Rajesh's ID card at the entrance to confirm he really is Rajesh. Authorization is the rulebook that then decides which rooms his badge may open. Even if his ID is genuine, a note in the rulebook saying "this person must never enter the vault" overrides every permission — that is the explicit deny winning. If no rule mentions a room at all, the default is that the door stays locked — that is the implicit deny.

**One line to remember:** Authentication proves who you are, authorization decides what you may do, and in IAM an explicit deny beats an explicit allow, which beats the default implicit deny.

sections.s2_technical:
Authentication in AWS happens before any policy is read. For a human it is a console password, optionally with multi-factor authentication. For a program it is a cryptographic signature (SigV4) on the request made with access keys, or a session token from STS. If the signature or token is invalid, the request is rejected immediately with an authentication error — authorization is never even consulted.

Once authenticated, AWS performs authorization. It gathers every policy that applies to the request: identity-based policies on the User, Group, and Role; resource-based policies on the target such as an S3 bucket policy; permission boundaries; service control policies at the organization level; and session policies. It then evaluates them with a strict order of precedence.

The order is the part interviewers test. First, if any policy contains an explicit deny that matches the action and resource, the request is denied, full stop — nothing can override an explicit deny. Second, if there is no explicit deny but at least one policy contains a matching allow, the request is permitted. Third, if nothing matches at all, the default is an implicit deny, so the request is refused. In short, everything is denied by default, an allow opens it, and an explicit deny slams it shut again.

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:*", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::nbi-statements/*" },
    { "Effect": "Deny",  "Action": "s3:DeleteObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::nbi-statements/*" }
  ]
}
```

In this policy the holder can do everything on the statements bucket except delete objects, because the explicit deny on `s3:DeleteObject` overrides the broad allow. This is the standard way to grant wide access while carving out a few forbidden actions, which in banking is how we let a service read and write statements but never delete them.

A senior nuance: in AWS Organizations a service control policy that omits an action acts like a ceiling — even if an account's own policy allows it, the request fails if the SCP does not permit it. SCPs filter the maximum permissions; they do not grant anything by themselves.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A back-office service at National Bank of India needs full read and write on the statements bucket so it can generate and update PDFs, but it must be impossible for it to delete a statement, because deleted statements are an audit and compliance disaster. This is exactly what explicit deny beating explicit allow solves: grant broad access, then deny the one dangerous action.

Problem 2 — An unknown action that no policy mentions must be refused by default. This is exactly what implicit deny provides: if no statement matches, the answer is no.

We will build a `PolicyEngine` that implements the real precedence. Classes: `Statement` (effect, action, resource), `PolicyEngine.evaluate(...)` returning ALLOW or DENY, and an `Authenticator` that first proves identity before authorization runs.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the back-office service presenting a valid STS token, plus a policy that allows all S3 actions on the statements bucket but denies delete.

Step 1 — Authentication runs first. The `Authenticator` checks the token starts with `valid-`. It does, so the identity is proven. If the token were invalid, the request would stop here with an authentication failure and authorization would never run.

Step 2 — The service asks to PutObject. The `PolicyEngine` scans the statements. The `s3:*` allow matches PutObject, no deny matches it, so the result is ALLOW.

Step 3 — The service asks to GetObject. Same path: the broad allow matches, no deny matches, so ALLOW.

Step 4 — The service asks to DeleteObject. The broad allow matches, but the explicit Deny on `s3:DeleteObject` also matches. Because explicit deny wins immediately, the engine returns DENY without even considering the allow.

Step 5 — The service asks to GetObject on a different bucket. No statement mentions that bucket, so nothing matches and the result is the implicit DENY.

```
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Authentication (who are you?) succeeded: true
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Can PutObject?  ALLOW
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Can GetObject?  ALLOW
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [WARNING] Can DeleteObject? DENY (explicit deny wins)
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [WARNING] Can access other bucket? DENY (implicit — nothing matched)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Request: principal=back-office-svc, action=s3:DeleteObject
    │
    ▼
  Authentication (SigV4 / STS token valid?)
    │ invalid ──→ 403 AuthN error (stop, no authz)
    │ valid
    ▼
  Authorization — gather all policies
    │
    ├─ explicit DENY matches?  ── yes ──→ DENY (final)
    │                              no
    ├─ explicit ALLOW matches? ── yes ──→ ALLOW
    │                              no
    └─ nothing matches ─────────────────→ implicit DENY
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Policy Evaluation Engine ═══

  ┌─ Patterns ─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Chain-of-precedence: deny short-circuits, allow latches │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: Authenticator authenticates; PolicyEngine authorizes  │
  │ O: new effects or conditions extend Statement.matches    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌───────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │ Authenticator │        │ PolicyEngine            │
  │ + authenticate│        │ + evaluate(stmts,a,r)   │
  └───────────────┘        └───────────┬─────────────┘
                                       │ uses *
                                       ▼
                             ┌─────────────────────┐
                             │ Statement           │
                             │ - effect,action,res │
                             │ + matches(a,r)      │
                             └─────────────────────┘

  Contract for evaluate(stmts, action, resource):
    Pre:  authentication already succeeded
    Post: DENY if any explicit deny matches
          ALLOW if an allow matches and no deny
          DENY otherwise (implicit)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Authentication and authorization are two separate steps that people often blur together. Authentication is proving who you are — for a human it is a password with multi-factor, and for a program it is a cryptographic signature on the request or a session token from STS. If that fails, AWS rejects the request immediately and never even looks at permissions. Authorization is the second step: now that AWS knows who you are, it decides what you are allowed to do by evaluating the IAM policies that apply.

The evaluation follows a strict and memorable order of precedence. AWS gathers every applicable policy — the identity policies on the User, Group, and Role, any resource policy like an S3 bucket policy, permission boundaries, and organization service control policies — and then it applies three rules. First, if any policy has an explicit deny that matches, the request is denied and nothing can override it. Second, if there is no explicit deny but at least one allow matches, the request is permitted. Third, if nothing matches at all, the default is an implicit deny. So everything is denied by default, an allow opens the door, and an explicit deny slams it shut no matter what.

In banking this precedence is extremely useful. At National Bank of India our back-office service needs broad read and write access to the statements bucket so it can generate and update PDFs, but it must be impossible for it to delete a statement, because a deleted statement is an audit and compliance disaster. So we write one policy that allows all S3 actions on the bucket and a second statement that explicitly denies the delete action. The explicit deny overrides the broad allow, giving us wide access with a surgical exception.

One senior point I always add is about AWS Organizations. A service control policy acts as a ceiling, not a grant — if the SCP does not permit an action, it fails even when the account's own policy allows it, but the SCP never grants anything by itself. Understanding that identity policies, resource policies, and SCPs all feed into the same deny-beats-allow-beats-implicit-deny evaluation is what shows an interviewer I understand how real access decisions are made across a whole banking organization.
